roots.name: 74-series glue logic
roots.description: The off-the-shelf logic chips on a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 that are not Commodore's own designs - thirteen positions according to the service-manual parts list, plus an LM556 timer alongside them. They do no arithmetic and no video: they multiplex addresses, latch bytes, decode chip selects, count, generate the video dot clock and invert the cassette port. Ten are 74-series in black epoxy DIP, three are CMOS 4000-series, and the U8 is an older non-Schottky 7406. Individually each was a commodity costing tens of cents.
roots.note: The part list below is taken from the official C64 Service Manual parts list for PCB assembly #250407 and independently corroborated by three hobbyist references (Retrogate's retro.rewind wiki, the C64-Wiki motherboard page, and MonkeySpeak's hardware detail sheet). It is NOT the list that circulates in most '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' compilations (74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125, 74LS181, 74LS14, 74LS04, 74LS00) - those part numbers belong to the Apple II, the VIC-20 and the BBC Micro, not the C64; see the '74-series parts that are NOT on a C64' node below. One widely-copied web page (oldsilicon.com) swaps the 74LS257 and the 74LS373 between U14 and U26; the service manual says U14 = 74LS258 and U26 = 74LS373, which this tree follows, and the 74LS258 node records the discrepancy in its own note. There is also a count discrepancy worth knowing: the frequently quoted 'eleven glue chips' does not reconcile with the parts list. The service manual gives ten packages carrying a 74 prefix - U8, U13, U14, U15, U25, U26, U27, U29, U30, U31 - and three CMOS packages, U16, U28 and U32, which is thirteen positions before the LM556 is counted at all. That is twelve distinct part numbers, because the 74LS257 is fitted twice and the 4066 twice. On the shape of the branch: each chip's `children` are the bipolar process and the DIP package, which is a manufacturing decomposition rather than strict containment, but it is the decomposition every other subsystem in this tree uses for a bought component, and the commodity materials hang off `inputs` so they resolve to the canonical metal.* and chem.* nodes instead of being inlined.

facts.value: 10 packages, 8 distinct part numbers (the 74LS257 is fitted twice)

facts.label: CMOS parts fitted
facts.value: 4 packages, 3 distinct part numbers (4066 x2, MC4044, 74LS629)

facts.label: Distinct part numbers

children.name: 7406 hex inverter buffer, open collector (U8)
children.description: Six inverting buffers whose outputs are open collectors rather than totem poles, in a 14-pin DIP. On the 250407 they invert and buffer the 6510's cassette-port output lines (CASS MOTOR, CASS SENSE, CASS WRITE, CASS DATA) and the shared user-port / serial lines. Open-collector outputs with pull-ups are how those lines could be wired-OR and level-shifted without contention, and a pin that shorts to ground leaves the CPU reading the defined 'off' state rather than floating.
children.note: The service manual lists U8 as '7406 sub 7416'. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the MOS house-number part 7707, and those MOS-made 'equivalent' parts are notoriously unreliable - a 7406/7707 failing high is a classic cause of a dead datasette or a stuck serial bus. Confidence is medium on the exact nets driven; high on the part number and function class.

children.name: 74LS257 quad 2-to-1 multiplexer (U13 and U25)
children.description: Two identical 16-pin packages, each holding four independent 2-to-1 data selectors with non-inverting outputs. They exist for one reason: the 4164 DRAMs are multiplexed parts with only nine address pins, taking a row address first and a column address a few hundred nanoseconds later on the same wires. The CPU has sixteen address bits to deliver, so eight of them have to be time-division multiplexed onto four wires. One 74LS257 multiplexes four bits; two are needed for eight.
children.note: A 74LS257 differs from a 74LS258 only in having totem-pole (push-pull) outputs instead of three-state outputs. This distinction is why U13/U25 and U14 do different jobs.

facts.label: Select inputs
facts.value: 1 per 2-to-1 selector, shared by the two selectors of each 4-bit nibble

children.name: 74LS258 quad multiplexer with three-state outputs (U14)
children.description: The same four 2-to-1 selectors as the 74LS257 but with outputs that can be switched into a high-impedance state. This is the bus arbiter for VIC-II memory access: when the VIC-II is allowed to take the bus, the multiplexer's outputs are disabled so the VIC-II's own address pins can drive directly instead of fighting them. A failed U14 shows up as the VIC-II being unable to fetch screen data from RAM.
children.note: Some third-party board listings incorrectly give U14 as a 74LS373. The Commodore service manual parts list for #250407 says 74LS258.

children.name: 74LS139 dual 1-of-4 decoder (U15)
children.description: Two independent four-way decoders with common active-low enables and active-low outputs, in a 16-pin DIP. Given four address bits and an enable, each half asserts exactly one of four outputs. Commodore uses it to expand the sparse decode coming out of the PLA into individual chip selects - VIC-II banking, the I/O devices - and to qualify them with the read/write phase. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the house-number part 7708/7711.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). The exact set of selects it generates is medium confidence because most of the C64's address decoding lives in the 82S100 PLA at U17, and secondary sources disagree about which outputs the 74LS139 finishes off. MOS house-number versions of this decoder were a notorious C64 failure; they are more fragile than the TI/Fairchild/National parts.

children.name: 74LS373 octal D latch, three-state (U26)
children.description: Eight transparent D-type latches with three-state outputs in a 20-pin DIP. The VIC-II has only eight address pins but must reach two different memories - the 1 KB screen/bitmap RAM and the character-generator ROM - so it puts one byte on its own pins while this latch holds the other byte. The three-state outputs let the CPU read the latched byte back whenever the VIC is not driving. A dead U26 corrupts text and bitmap graphics but leaves everything else alive, which is why it is the classic 'screen is garbage but the machine boots' fault.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: octal transparent latch with three-state outputs

children.name: 74LS08 quad 2-input AND gate (U27)
children.description: Four independent two-input AND gates in a 14-pin DIP - the most ordinary chip on the board and the one that does the most unglamorous work. ANDing is how the machine makes qualified control signals: a decode line ANDed with a clock phase becomes /RAS, /CAS or /WE for the DRAMs, and ANDed with the read/write phase becomes the chip select for the VIC-II, SID or CIA. Commodore also second-sourced it as house-number part 7712.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The specific AND terms are inferred from the topology of a dynamic-RAM controller rather than read off the schematic net by net, hence medium.

children.name: 74LS74 dual D-type flip-flop (U29)
children.description: Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with asynchronous preset and clear, in a 14-pin DIP. In the C64 they sit in the DRAM timing chain: shaping and stretching the column strobe and dividing or retiming the phase clock so the 4164s get a valid /CAS pulse on the right edge. A flip-flop is what turns a combinational AND into a one-shot wide enough to meet the memory's timing spec.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The functional description is low confidence: hobbyist references variously call U29 a 'divider', a 'dual D-type flip-flop', and part of the VIC-II raster timing, and the 251138 schematic was not traced net by net to settle it.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual D positive-edge-triggered flip-flop with preset and clear

children.name: 74LS193 synchronous 4-bit up/down counter (U30)
children.description: A four-bit presettable binary counter with separate up and down clocks and a clear, in a 16-pin DIP. It sequences the multiplexed dynamic-RAM cycle - stepping through address states and generating the refresh strobes - and helps step the VIC-II's raster counters. This is the chip that turns 'one address bit is high right now' into 'we are on the nth step of a cycle'.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). Its exact role is low confidence: sources call it a 'binary counter', a divider, and part of the clock-generation chain, and the 250407 does share a cluster of counters and flip-flops (U29/U30) around the DRAM and raster timing that is hard to allocate from the parts list alone.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: synchronous presettable 4-bit up/down binary counter with clear

children.name: 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (U31)
children.description: Two voltage-controlled oscillator sections plus an enable and a range control, in a 14-pin DIP. The C64 has no crystal governing its video dot clock: one half of U31 amplifies the colour-subcarrier reference coming out of the video circuitry, the other half generates a free-running dot clock whose frequency is pulled by a control voltage. That is the oscillator half of the phase-locked loop completed by the MC4044 at U32. Despite the 'LS' prefix this part is CMOS internally, not bipolar TTL.
children.note: Part number, position and PLL role are high confidence and corroborated by scope measurements of the 250407 clock circuit published at tech.guitarsite.de/c64_scope.html. That the 74LS624-629 family is fabricated in CMOS rather than bipolar TTL despite the LS prefix is medium confidence: the family descends from Signetics/National designs and behaves like CMOS in pinout and power-up, but no period datasheet sentence stating the process has been found. Some vendors did not offer it at all, which is itself suggestive.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual voltage-controlled oscillator with enable and range control

children.name: CMOS logic on the board: 4066 switches and MC4044
children.description: Four of the C64's glue chips are CMOS rather than bipolar TTL: two 4066 quad bilateral switches (U16, U28) and one MC4044 phase/frequency comparator (U32), plus the 74LS629 above. The 4066 is four independent CMOS transmission gates used as analogue multiplexers to route luma, chroma and audio and to hand the shared pins between the VIC-II and the outside world. The MC4044 compares the VCO's phase against the colour-subcarrier reference and generates the control voltage that locks the dot clock. Both were Motorola/RCA 4000-series parts, normally sold as CD4066B and CD4044B.
children.note: These are 4000-series CMOS, not 7400-series, so strictly they sit outside a '74-series' scope. They are included because they are the clearest demonstration that a single 1983 Commodore board carried two completely different semiconductor processes, and because the brief asked for the CMOS branch to be covered from a real machine.

facts.label: Named suppliers
facts.value: Motorola (MC prefix), RCA/Intersil (CD prefix), TI CD-prefix

children.name: LM556 dual timer (U20) - adjacent, not a logic part
children.simple_name: LM556 dual timer U20, not logic
children.description: Two 555-class monostable timers sharing one package, in a 14-pin DIP. It sits in the analogue paddle-input path, producing the timed pulse whose width the SID measures to report joystick and paddle position. Included here for completeness because it is off-the-shelf, because it is bipolar, and because it was made on the same diffusion lines as the TTL glue - just a different circuit on them.
children.note: An analogue bipolar part, not a 7400-series logic IC. Its internal process is a linear bipolar flow - epitaxial collector, deep wide-base, large-area emitters, no Schottky clamps and no thin-film resistor level - rather than the junction-isolated Schottky logic flow the bipolar branch describes.

children.name: 74-series parts that are NOT on a C64
children.description: A warning about the part list, kept so a reader can trust the sibling nodes. Frequently published lists of '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' include 74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125 and 74LS181. None of those are on the ASSY 250407. They belong to other machines - the 74LS181 look-ahead carry and the 74LS165 shift registers are Apple II parts, the 74LS157 multiplexers are VIC-20 and BBC Micro parts - and they are almost always the result of copying a generic 'TTL in home computers' list rather than reading a parts list. This is commentary about the supply chain, not an entity, so it is a note.
children.note: Which machine each wrongly-attributed part actually belongs to is a verified finding, held at medium confidence. Twelve of the parts really are fitted to the ASSY 250407.

children.name: The black epoxy DIP
children.description: Nearly every 74-series chip Commodore bought arrived in a black moulded dual in-line package: a lead frame carrying sixteen to twenty pins on 0.1 in centres, a piece of die glued to the frame's centre paddle, a fan of 0.5 mil gold wires, and about a third of a gram of filled epoxy poured over the whole thing and cured. This is the single most replicated package in electronics history. The 0.100 in lead pitch fits cheap single-row sockets and perforated-board grids, and the 0.3 in row spacing up to 24 pins (0.6 in above) balances insertion stiffness against footprint.

facts.label: Row spacing
facts.value: 0.3 in (7.62 mm) for 14-24 pin; 0.6 in (15.24 mm) for 28/40 pin

facts.label: Bond wire
facts.value: 0.7-1.0 mil gold, ~20 bonds for a 20-pin DIP

children.name: 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) lead pitch
children.description: The distance between adjacent pins on one row of the DIP. It is the same pitch as the holes on a piece of perforated board, and it is the reason a 74LS04 could be dropped into a socket or a perfboard without any special tooling. The pin itself is a 0.25 x 0.5 mm rectangular wire, the narrow dimension facing the chip.

facts.label: Lead length (DIP-14)
facts.value: ~7.6 mm from body shoulder to tip

children.name: 0.3 inch row spacing and its wider variants
children.description: The distance between the two rows of pins. Standard JEDEC practice in 1983 was 300 mil for packages up to 24 pins and 600 mil for 28-pin and 40-pin parts, so a 40-pin device and a 16-pin device could share a footprint grid. A 900 mil (22.9 mm) body was used by some hermetic and high-current ceramic parts but was never common in merchant logic.
children.note: The 0.3 in / 0.6 in rule is high confidence; the existence of a 0.9 in (22.9 mm) row spacing in the same era is medium confidence - such spacings appear on hermetic and high-power ceramic packages, but none has been confirmed on a merchant logic part.

children.name: Nickel-iron lead frame
children.description: A continuous strip of metal, punched and formed into a repeating chain of DIP skeletons joined by tie-bars. It arrives at the assembler as a reel of maybe 3000 frames; the frames are cut out one at a time, plated, and then become the skeleton of the package - the seventeen or more separate pins, the two rows, and the little central ledge the die sits on.
children.note: Carpenter 45 (42% Ni / 58% Fe, balance carbon and manganese) and similar low-expansion nickel-iron alloys were the standard logic lead frame material because the thermal expansion coefficient was tuned to match the alumina-and-epoxy package, so the die, the frame and the mould compound do not fight each other over temperature cycling. It was a commodity ferronickel-like alloy made in ordinary steel melts - the same order of chemistry as the ferronickel made from laterite in the metals branch, but at 42% Ni rather than 60-75%, and made to a coefficient spec rather than to a nickel content spec.

facts.label: Iron fraction
facts.value: ~58 wt% - the majority of the frame by mass, and commodity steel

children.name: Copper-clad C4 lead frame (later, not 1983)
children.description: A lead frame fabricated not from a bulk alloy strip but from an aluminium or copper leadframe clad on both faces with a controlled thickness of copper, so the surface the solder sees is copper rather than a flash plate. Known by the trademark C4. It solved the tin-whisker and solderability problems at once and became standard for fine-pitch packages from the late 1980s onward.
children.note: Included to mark the boundary: a C64 from 1983 contains no C4 frames. The technology existed in the late 1980s but was not standard on through-hole merchant logic. Copper is an ingredient, so it hangs off `inputs` rather than as a child.

children.name: The separated, tested die
children.description: Between the diffusion bay and the packaging line, the wafer is scribed into rectangles, diced, and every rectangle is probed while still in wafer form. The die that arrives at the assembly line is a bare rectangle of silicon, perhaps 1.5 by 2.5 mm, with a scratched pattern of aluminium bonding pads on one face and a bare oxide film over the circuitry on the other.

children.name: Why 4164 DRAMs die but 74LS parts mostly do not
children.description: A 74LS gate is a handful of transistors with enormous margin; it either works or the diffusion is cracked. A 64Kx1 DRAM stores charge in a capacitor about 100 femtofarads across a transistor with a leakage path, and it has to be refreshed every few milliseconds. That is why the eight 4164s on the C64 are the board's failure-prone chips and the 74-series glue is almost always fine.
children.note: The mechanism (charge storage and refresh) is high confidence; the comparative failure rate is a well-attested field observation rather than a measured statistic.

children.name: The ceramic DIP (mostly not used here)
children.description: For military and extended-temperature parts the epoxy was replaced by a package made of alumina ceramic, sealed hermetically with a glass frit or a metal lid. It could be baked out, leak-tested, and taken from -55 to +125 C without the epoxy softening. It was also more expensive and much larger, so merchant logic in a home computer was always plastic: the C64's own 74-series parts are all black epoxy, with the ceramic version only appearing in industrial or aerospace equipment.
children.note: The 74LS series exists in both CDIP (ceramic) and PDIP (plastic) forms, distinguished by the letter after the temperature grade: N is plastic (0 to +70 C), E or M is ceramic (-55 to +125 C). Commodore specified N-grade parts.

children.name: Kovar lid and nickel seal ring
children.simple_name: Kovar lid and nickel seal ring
children.description: For parts sealed with metal rather than glass, a lid of Kovar (iron-nickel-cobalt, chosen for its matching expansion) is brazed or welded to a nickel ring around the ceramic. Kovar is the same idea as the lead frame alloy: pick the expansion coefficient of the metal so it matches the ceramic and the seal does not crack.

children.name: How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)
children.description: The 74LS family was not built on the same kind of line as the Commodore custom chips. This is a junction-isolated, collector-diffused bipolar process: an n+ buried-and-collector structure grown epitaxially on p-type silicon, four thermal diffusion cycles, a sputtered NiCr resistor level, one level of aluminium metallisation, about eight mask levels and sixty to a hundred process steps. Minimum drawn features were 3-5 um - twenty times coarser than a 1983 dynamic RAM - which is exactly why a logic chip cost a fraction of what a 6510 or a 4164 cost.
children.note: This is a generalised description of the standard junction-isolated bipolar logic process as it was run in 1982-84 by TI, Fairchild, National and Motorola. Precise vendors differed: Fairchild also offered a dielectric-isolation variant, and TI ran some processes with ion implantation instead of thermal base diffusion. Confidence is medium rather than high, because the 74LS flows are proprietary and no period process description for a specific vendor's 74LS line has been seen. The transistor structure, the four-diffusion sequence, the NiCr resistor level and the eight mask levels are all well documented industry practice for the era. The resulting geometry is a 0.5-1 um base and a 1-2 um emitter inside an isolation island a few tens of micrometres across, wired with 3-5 um aluminium on one level. For comparison, the 4164 DRAM on the same board was patterned at around 1-2 um with two or three aluminium levels, and the VIC-II and SID at around 2-3 um with two levels, which is why a DRAM cost more than the glue.

facts.label: Diffusion cycles
facts.value: 4 thermal: isolation, base, emitter, plus the epitaxial growth itself

facts.label: Interconnect
facts.value: single aluminium level + sputtered NiCr resistor

facts.label: 4164 DRAM, same era
facts.value: ~1-2 um, two or three metal levels

facts.label: Custom VIC-II / SID NMOS, same era

children.name: Cleanroom air, filtration and the wet bench
children.description: The whole front end runs in filtered air with positive pressure, and the wet benches - the sinks where wafers are etched and cleaned - were the dirtiest place in the fab and the reason it needed a Class 100 (ISO 5) hood over every one. HEPA-filtered air was blown down continuously; nitrogen and dry air purged the tool chambers; and huge volumes of deionised water and process chemicals flowed through the sinks.

facts.label: Classes used
facts.value: Class 10 (ISO 4) mask bay, Class 100 (ISO 5) sub-fab and diffusion bay, Class 1000 (ISO 6) wet bays

facts.label: Wet benches
facts.value: polypropylene sinks under Class 100 laminar hoods

children.note: Two nodes were folded into this one in QA. First, the photomask bay, which had been a separate facility child of the photolithography process: coating, exposing and developing happened in a yellow room under filtered mercury light and then in a Class 10 (ISO 4) mini-environment with the aligners under hoods, and it was the largest bay in the building by machine count and by electricity draw after the cleanroom air itself. It belonged here rather than under a process step. Second, the bulk process gases - nitrogen for purging tool chambers and for the sinter anneal, hydrogen for the metal anneal, oxygen for oxidation and for ashing photoresist, dry nitrogen also as the blow-off gas for every wafer before it entered a hot tool - which were a separate child duplicating chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases and are now named in `inputs`. Note on the older US class numbering: Class 100 = ISO 5, Class 1000 = ISO 6, Class 10 = ISO 4; it is a different convention from the ISO class numbers used today. Bulk gases, water and power are cross-cutting services and are `from` edges, not components of the building.

children.name: The merchant logic fab that ran the process
children.description: A 1983 merchant logic line was a long building with a linear flow: wafers came in at the front and moved one way through cleaning, oxidation and diffusion, photolithography, etch and metallisation, then out to probe, then to assembly and test at the back. Because a logic process was so repeatable, one fab ran dozens of different part numbers on the same flow, changing only the mask set - which is exactly why the 74LS catalogue was so cheap.
children.note: That the process ran in a clean room inside a dedicated fab is documented, and that a single process serves many part numbers. Not established: the linear bay layout and its bay order, the water, power and nitrogen as services, the vendor plant list, or that one mask set per part number is why the catalogue was cheap.

children.name: Oxidation and diffusion bay
children.description: The hot end of the fab: tube furnaces for oxidation, source drive-in and anneal, plus the epitaxial reactors. This bay determined the cycle time of the whole line, because a diffusion push is hours and a furnace boat takes 20-40 wafers. An operator loaded boats in and out at a slow, deliberate rhythm all shift.

children.name: Metallisation bay
children.description: The vacuum tool room: the sputterers that lay down the NiCr resistors and the aluminium metal, the evaporation stations, the sinter furnace, and the ion-implantation machines. Vacuum and cleanroom in one room; argon flows constantly.
children.note: Not established: that sputterers, evaporators, a sinter furnace and ion implanters shared one vacuum tool room with argon flowing, or any of the equipment inventory. Sputtering and evaporation are documented as techniques; the bay is a layout assumption.

children.name: Fab utilities: water, power, scrubbers
children.description: A logic fab in 1983 drew tens of megawatts and consumed tens of millions of gallons of ultrapure water a year, and every acid vapour had to be scrubbed. The ultrapure water plant - reverse osmosis then ion exchange, then a final 0.2 um filter - was as large and as capital-intensive as any single machine in the fab.
children.note: The scale figures are order-of-magnitude for a large logic fab, not verified for a specific plant. Water intensity for semiconductors is high relative to most manufacturing; this is well documented generally. Water and power are named in `inputs`, so they render as `from` edges: following this node's materials should not drag a water treatment plant into a logic supply line.

children.name: What happened to bipolar logic afterwards
children.description: The 74LS line described here is essentially extinct as a manufacturing process. CMOS won because it drew almost no static power, scaled, and could hold a whole microprocessor on one die, which bipolar could never do economically. Bipolar survives only in niches - power regulators, high-voltage controllers, low-dropout rectifiers, precision amplifiers, the front end of high-speed analog, microwave amplifiers, Hall sensors - where the transistor's current handling and gain are still hard to beat, and those parts are still grown epitaxially and still use guard rings and deep-trench isolation at the leading edge: the process family survived, the market for plain logic gates in it did not. The two families briefly merged in BiCMOS, which built CMOS logic and bipolar output drivers on the same die for gate arrays and for the output stages of older CPUs; it was abandoned once CMOS could drive high current on its own, and is largely gone from production. And the geometry is unrecognisable: the 3-5 um feature of this line put of the order of 10^1 to 10^2 transistors on a die, where a modern GPU puts about 10^10, on 300 mm wafers. Nothing about the aluminium DIP package, the epoxy, the lead frame or the 0.1 in pitch changed at all through that entire scaling - only the silicon inside.
children.note: Three things are worth knowing after following the 1983 flow: which niches bipolar logic survives in, what BiCMOS was, and how far the geometry has moved since.

facts.label: 2020s logic
facts.value: nanometre nodes, ~10^10 transistors per die on a 300 mm wafer

facts.label: Unchanged by all of it
facts.value: DIP package, epoxy moulding, lead frame, 0.1 in lead pitch

children.name: The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629
children.description: Three of the C64's glue chips are CMOS, and they were made on a completely different line from the 74LS parts. Instead of four diffusion cycles and an epitaxial collector, a CMOS line does a p-well and an n-well implant, grows a field oxide between them by LOCOS, grows a hundred-nanometre gate oxide, deposits polysilicon, and uses that same polysilicon as its own mask for the source and drain implant. Roughly ten mask levels, no epitaxy, no gold, no NiCr resistor film, and a static power consumption of nanowatts instead of milliwatts. That combination is why CMOS took the whole logic business within fifteen years.
children.note: Describes a 3-5 um n-well/p-well twin-tub CMOS process with LOCOS isolation, self-aligned source/drain and a single aluminium level - the mainstream logic CMOS of 1982-84, and the process behind the RCA/Motorola 4000-series and the early 74HC. TI's Micralign lines, Fairchild's and National's equivalent lines, and the Japanese and Korean fabs all ran something close to this. Two details are period-specific: LOCOS was still the isolation of choice (shallow-trench isolation was arriving but not yet dominant), and the 4000-series parts such as the 4066 and MC4044 were older designs that typically used a simpler, single-well or p-well-only CMOS rather than a full twin-tub. Confidence medium because the exact flow of a given vendor's 4000-series part is proprietary.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: n-well / p-well twin-tub CMOS, LOCOS isolation

facts.label: Minimum feature
facts.value: 3-5 um (same node as the bipolar logic line)

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: polysilicon over ~100 nm thermal oxide, self-aligned S/D

facts.label: Static power
facts.value: nW per gate vs ~2 mW for a 74LS gate

children.name: CMOS transmission gate (bilateral switch)
children.description: The 4066's four bilateral switches are the canonical CMOS cell: two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel between two nodes, each with its gate driven by one of the two control inputs. When the control is high the pair conducts in both directions; when it is low the pair is off and the terminals float. It is two transistors. That is the whole reason CMOS logic is cheap - there is no junction isolation, no epitaxy, no resistor film and no gold-doped emitter to reproduce for every function, just NMOS and PMOS. It is also why the 4066 could be used as an analogue multiplexer at all: the on-resistance of a few hundred ohms to a few kilohm was low enough to route luma, chroma and audio, where a single bipolar pass transistor would have cost more than the rest of the gate.
children.note: The transmission-gate cell is a real object - two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel is what the 4066 is actually made of.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: complementary NMOS + PMOS in parallel = transmission gate

facts.label: Bidirectional
facts.value: yes - unlike an NMOS pass transistor

facts.label: On resistance
facts.value: hundreds of ohms to a few kohm

children.name: What CMOS became
children.description: The same n-well/p-well/twin-tub idea, shrunk by a factor of thousands. Every design rule changed. The bird's beak - the way LOCOS field oxide grew sideways and swallowed the active area - became a scaling killer, and shallow trench isolation, in which a narrow trench is etched into the substrate and filled with oxide over a nitride liner, gave a much sharper boundary and became universal from the late 1980s onward; STI is itself a direct descendant of the deep-trench-isolation idea that appeared at the high-performance end of the bipolar branch, so the two halves of this tree converged on the same solution. STI in turn gave way to fin-shaped gates and gate-all-around. The gate material changed from polysilicon to metal. The number of copper interconnect layers went from one to a dozen. The light source went from a mercury lamp at 436 nm to an argon-fluoride excimer laser at 193 nm, and then to extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, which needs a vacuum. A 3-5 um logic gate became a nanometre-scale device with billions of its relatives.
children.note: Shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS: a narrow trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide over a nitride liner, giving a much sharper boundary than the bird's beak.

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: LOCOS -> shallow trench -> finFET and gate-all-around

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: 436 nm mercury lamp -> 193 nm ArF -> 13.5 nm EUV

facts.label: Transistors per die
facts.value: ~10 for a 4066 switch; ~10^10 for a modern GPU

children.name: Merchant logic supply to Commodore
children.description: Commodore did not fab logic. It bought merchant 74-series parts from the American and Japanese vendors, and because a machine built in millions cannot wait for a part number to be on allocation, it also ran second sources of its own - internal house-numbered equivalents made at other plants, marked 7701, 7707, 7708, 7711, 8712 and so on. An original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore number, all mixed on the same board, all doing the same job. This branch describes Commodore's procurement rather than a physical process: the vendors are companies, the second-source parts are a real component family, and the distribution chain is a sentence about how parts travelled rather than a thing.
children.note: The vendor list and the second-source practice are well attested by the physical parts on surviving boards and by Commodore's parts lists. Not established: which plants made Commodore's specific lots, so no plant is claimed below as fact.

facts.label: Named suppliers on a 250407
facts.value: TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba, MOS house numbers

facts.label: Purchase route
facts.value: vendor sales, franchised distributor, and broker / open market

children.name: The merchant logic vendors
children.description: Five or six companies made the overwhelming majority of the world's 74-series logic in the early 1980s. Between them they ran the same public process to the same design rules, which is why a 74LS08 from any of them was interchangeable. What they did not share was quality: this is the core of the C64's running joke that some boards need three attempts before they work. The companies themselves are the entities here; this framing paragraph is commentary, so the node is a note that keeps them as children.
children.note: The observation worth carrying is the one a company list cannot show on its own: the six ran the same public process to the same design rules, so their parts were interchangeable, but not equally well made.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: TI invented the 7400; Fairchild, National and Motorola/Signetics cloned and improved it

facts.label: Interchangeability
facts.value: same pinout and function, different vendor mark

children.name: Commodore's house-numbered second sources
children.description: To avoid single-supplier risk Commodore had equivalents of several glue parts made for it and marked with its own house numbers: 7701 and 8701 in place of the PLA family, 7707 for the 7406 hex inverter, 7708 or 7711 for the 74LS139 decoder, and 7712 for the 74LS08 quad AND. These were contracted from other fabs under Commodore's specification. They are functionally equivalent and reliably much worse - the MOS-made decoder and inverter parts are among the most failure-prone components on a C64. This node records the practice and the part numbers rather than being one of the parts itself: the four house numbers are four different devices in four different packages, so there is no single object here to put in a box.
children.note: What this records is the equivalence between Commodore's house numbers and the standard 74-series parts they stand in for, not any single device: the four numbers are four different devices in four different packages.

facts.value: equivalent to the 7406 hex inverter at U8
equivalent to the 74LS139 decoder at U15
equivalent to the 74LS08 quad AND at U27

facts.label: Reliability
facts.value: the MOS house-number parts are notably failure-prone

children.name: How the chips physically arrived in 1983
children.description: Nobody at Commodore's Pennsylvania assembly plant picked up a telephone and ordered from Texas Instruments. There was a distribution chain, and where a part sat in that chain decided both its price and whether it was genuine. Buying from the manufacturer's own sales arm or a franchised distributor got you an authorised part with a full warranty and a date code. Buying from a broker or an independent distributor got you the same silicon much cheaper, with no guarantee of origin at all. Three mechanisms made the difference. Allocation: when demand exceeded supply - and in 1982-84 it very often did, because the whole consumer electronics industry was recovering from the 1980-81 recession simultaneously - a manufacturer rationed, a computer maker with a purchase order got whatever share the vendor allocated pro rata, and production had to be scheduled around delivery dates rather than around its own. That is why the price of a commodity 74LS was set by the market's shortage rather than by what it cost to make. Pulls: parts that reached a buyer through anything other than a franchised distributor were, in the trade's language, 'pulled', which could be entirely innocent - a company over-ordered and released surplus, a broker bought at auction - or diverted from a competitor's own allocation. Because a 74LS08 has no serial number, no authentication and no visible origin, nobody could tell the difference; the industry's response through the 1980s and 1990s was a growing formal apparatus for tracking authorised distribution, and the counterfeiting industry grew alongside it. And incoming inspection: every shipment of semiconductors was counted and checked against the bill of materials before the parts went near a board, with non-matching parts quarantined - which is worth noting because the components on a C64 mainboard are not hand-selected, so the board either works with whatever chip arrived in the box or it is reworked, which is a large part of why surviving C64s need a recap and a chip-sorting pass before they will run.
children.note: The franchised-versus-independent split, and the grey market that grew out of the early-1980s allocation shortages, are industry-level facts rather than properties of any one buyer.

facts.label: Unauthorised channels
facts.value: independent distributors, brokers, the open market

facts.label: Why the grey market existed
facts.value: allocation shortages, price gaps, and nobody policing small parts

facts.label: Allocation practice
facts.value: pro rata against a purchase order; 1982-84 was a shortage period

facts.label: Incoming inspection
facts.value: count and quarantine against the bill of materials; not hand-selection

children.name: What a 74LS is made of, and what it cost
children.description: The whole point of the comparison. A 74LS chip is a few milligrams of silicon, a few milligrams of metal, a third of a gram of epoxy, and a couple of hundred person-minutes of work spread across a fortnight of factory flow time. It sold for a few tens of cents. The 6510 on the same board, a thousand times more transistors on a finer process, cost several dollars. Commodore's entire bill of materials for the electronics was a small fraction of the machine's retail price. The bill of materials for one 74LS04, with the arithmetic: about 3 mg of silicon in a roughly 3.6 mm2 die cut from a 300 um wafer - the '3-5 um' figure usually quoted is the depth of the active junctions, not the mass; 10-30 mg of aluminium on the die from one 1.0-1.5 um level over about half the die area, which is an order of magnitude below the 0.3 g often quoted and is probably a wafer-level inventory figure rather than a per-chip one; under a milligram of gold in total, from about sixteen to twenty 0.5-1.0 mil wire bonds (0.2-0.4 mg) plus the die-attach preform (0.2-0.5 mg of Au-Si); under a milligram of sputtered NiCr; about 100 mg of nickel-iron in the lead frame at roughly 42 percent Ni, most of that mass being the iron half; and 0.3-0.6 g of silica-filled epoxy, three quarters of it fused silica. So the total is roughly half a gram per DIP-14, of which about 100:1 by mass is polymer, and the thirteen glue-chip positions on a C64 together weigh about six grams. The labour figure of roughly 200 person-minutes per finished chip is an order-of-magnitude estimate and worth unpacking, because it is not 200 minutes of one person's attention: it is direct operator and technician time amortised across the whole flow, roughly 20-30 operator touches across the 60-100 front-end steps, plus probe test, assembly, final test and inspection. Flow time is not touch time - a batch of wafers spends a week and a half moving through the fab, almost all of it waiting in a furnace, in a queue or in a cassette under a nitrogen purge, and what costs money is the twenty or thirty separate occasions when somebody has to be present and paying attention, which over a fortnight is a couple of hours. On price: a commodity 74LS gate was priced against a cost of a few tens of cents and a price in the same range, falling year on year as the industry learned; a merchant part's cost is amortised across every customer in the world and over a mask set that runs on a flow making dozens of other part numbers, so Commodore was buying a fraction of the output of a factory that existed whether or not Commodore existed, with a mask set it did not pay for and a design it did not own. The 6510 was the opposite on every count - one mask set, one customer, one buyer, a design that had to be paid for before it shipped a single unit - which is why Commodore's engineers minimised custom silicon and spent money freely on merchant glue, and also why the later C128 could add a second 6510 and a bank-switching PLA without touching the price of the machine.
children.note: Not established: a primary 1983 distributor price list for 74LS parts, a documented Commodore purchase price for a 6510, or a measured weight for any of these parts. Confidence is low on that basis. The 0.3 g of aluminium often quoted for a 14-pin logic chip is roughly an order of magnitude too high for the metal actually in the die. The mass figures are arithmetic from die dimensions and layer thicknesses and should be right to within a factor of a few; the price figures are order-of-magnitude estimates from the general semiconductor price decline of the era. The broader trend - prices falling roughly 10-30 percent a year in real terms through the early 1980s, faster for commodity logic - is documented in the economic literature and is the basis for the direction even where not the specific prices. Treat every number here as a defensible intuition rather than a measurement.

facts.value: ~3 mg (3.6 mm2 die x 300 um wafer)

facts.label: Aluminium on the die
facts.value: ~10-30 mg - the often-quoted 0.3 g looks like a wafer-level figure

facts.label: Gold per chip
facts.value: ~0.5-1 mg, from 16-20 wire bonds plus the die-attach preform

facts.label: The thirteen glue-chip positions on a C64
Direct labour
facts.value: ~100-300 person-minutes per finished device, across ~20-30 operator touches

facts.label: Flow time versus touch time
facts.value: ~1-2 weeks of factory time, of which hours are hands-on

facts.value: order 20-60 cents per 74LS (estimate); considerably less on volume contract
