mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu.name: The HEPA fan filter unit
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu.description: A box of pleated glass-fibre or PTFE media in a sheet-metal housing, blowing filtered air down over the tool at 20-40 air changes an hour. It is the single most numerous object in a 1980s fab - one every few square metres of ceiling - and it is why the whole building was pressurised and why the electricity bill was dominated by fan motors.

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.name: The wet bench
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.description: A row of acid-resistant sinks - quartz or polypropylene - where wafers are rinsed and wet-etched. Because wet chemistry releases acid mist and organic solvent vapour, every wet bench sat under a Class 100 laminar-flow hood and exhausted to a scrubbed stack. The wet bench is the reason a 1980s logic line was not as cheap to run as the 'it is just photolithography' story suggests.
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.note: Capital equipment, consumed slowly rather than used up in a single run. The nitrogen blow-off and the water flowing through the sinks are utilities supplied to the tool, not components of it.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.name: Boron oxide (B2O3) solid source
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.description: For thermal diffusion, boron was often carried in a boron-doped oxide or a boron nitride wafer placed face-to-face with the silicon in the diffusion boat. Cheaper and easier to handle than gas. The active species is boron oxide, B2O3; the name previously used here said 'borax', which is the sodium tetraborate and a different - and not the standard - source.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.note: Solid-source BN and doped-oxide diffusion was the classic boron diffusion technique before diborane became routine. Renamed from 'Borax / boron oxide source' because borax (Na2B4O7) is not what went in the boat. The gas source is no longer inlined here: chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane publishes diborane and boron trifluoride, which is more detailed than the one-sentence node that used to sit here.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Carbon black pigment
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: About half a percent by weight of furnace black, dispersed into the compound, to make the package opaque black. Black rather than natural-coloured because a black package hides internal voids, and because it was what the whole industry had standardised on since the first plastic DIP.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: The pigment is a trivial mass fraction of the whole computer but it is the same furnace black that goes into carbon-film resistors and into the photoconductor of a laser printer drum. Its feedstock is heavy petroleum residuum or natural gas fed to an air-cooled sooting furnace, the soot scraped off water-cooled rotors and pelletised.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Epoxy cresol novolac resin
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: The workhorse of chip packaging in every decade since 1970. Cresol-formaldehyde epoxy novolac is made from epichlorohydrin and a cresol-formaldehyde novolac; cured with a phenolic novolac and catalysed with a small amount of hexamethylenetetramine, it cures without volatiles and without ionising anything, so it does not damage the die. The epoxy end comes from epichlorohydrin, which industry has always made by chlorohydrination of propylene - propene plus hypochlorous acid to 1,2-dichloropropane, then base dehydrochlorination to close the epoxide ring - so the propylene came off a steam cracker, the chlorine out of a chlor-alkali cell, and the caustic soda out of the same cell: the plastic body of every 74LS chip traces back to salt and to crude oil.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: Bisphenol A epoxy (the older, less package-friendly EPON-type system) was still used on some parts; cresol novolac had largely displaced it in logic packaging. The epichlorohydrin -> propylene -> cracker -> chlorine -> brine chain used to be inlined beneath this node as seven nodes of its own; it is not inlined here. chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin publishes the molecule, chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3 the C3 stream, metal.chlorine and metal.chlor-alkali the chlorine, metal.salt-brine the brine and metal.caustic-soda the caustic. The chain is named by id in `inputs` so there is one copy of it in the tree.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: phenolic novolac + hexamine, 175 C, no by-products

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.name: The mask blank (soda-lime glass)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.description: A plate of low-expansion borosilicate or soda-lime glass, polished flat to a few micrometres over 150 mm. Low-expansion glass (LE glass) was preferred for masks because it did not change size with temperature. Both the blank and the pattern ultimately derive from fused silica.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.note: Silica is an ingredient of the blank, so metal.silica and metal.quartzite hang off `inputs` rather than as a child.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.name: The opaque chrome layer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.description: A layer of chromium, evaporated or sputtered onto the glass and then patterned by a mask writer. Chrome is used because it is opaque to the deep-UV and because it survives repeated contact printing without wearing. The clear areas are just bare glass, which is why a mask is easy to inspect: you look through it.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.note: Chromium is an ingredient of the mask, so metal.chromium hangs off `inputs` rather than as a child.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.name: Alumina ceramic body
mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.description: A package shell made of 95-99 percent alumina, formed by pressing or by tape-casting a green body in a serpentine conductor pattern and firing it at 1500-1600 C. Alumina was chosen because it matches silicon and the glass seal closely in expansion, is cheap, and is a good thermal conductor compared with any polymer.
mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.note: The bauxite-to-alumina route is not inlined here: metal.bauxite and metal.alumina publish it, with the caustic digestion and the ion-exchange steps on their side. Note that alumina reaches this package by two unrelated routes a few centimetres apart - as the ceramic body of a CDIP, and as the metal sputtered onto the die of the same part in its PDIP form.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.name: Eight masks, eight photolithography cycles
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.description: A full bipolar logic cycle is repeated for each of its eight mask levels, and each cycle is the same eight or nine operations: clean, dehydrate, spin-coat resist, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse and dry, hard-bake, then inspect - before the wafer goes back to the furnace, the etcher or the implanter. Eight masks times about nine operations is roughly seventy lithography operations, plus oxidation, etching and deposition steps that need no resist, giving the sixty-to-a-hundred total front-end steps.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.note: The mask set and its order in this tree: (1) isolation, (2) base, (3) NiCr resistor, (4) emitter, (5) contact window, (6) aluminium metal, (7) passivation window, plus the scribe/alignment level - about eight, ordering within the tree illustrative. Every mask is exposed once per wafer batch, and the whole flow through the diffusion and photolithography areas takes a batch of wafers roughly a week to ten days. Written out once, one mask level's cycle is ten operations - dehydrate, coat, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse, hard-bake, wet-etch, strip, clean - then the furnace or the sputterer; eight levels of ten is about eighty lithography-area operations, plus oxidation and diffusion pushes, plus metallisation, plus test. That count was a separate child node ('The full cycle, counted') and has been folded in here.

children.name: The mask set
children.description: A set of eight photomasks, one per level, each a square of glass about 15 cm on a side with the pattern for that level in opaque chrome. They are made once from the circuit layout, then used to print thousands of wafers. Making the mask set - patterning, mask inspection, and a few days of lead time - was itself a multi-thousand-dollar, multi-week undertaking, and the masks were the physical embodiment of the design.

children.name: The reticle (1:1 mask)
children.description: A bipolar logic wafer of 1983 was almost always patterned 1:1 by contact or proximity printing, so the mask carried the pattern at full size - a 100 mm wafer printed from a 100 mm mask. Reticles in the sense of 4x or 5x reduction masks were for steppers and mostly for the finer NMOS and DRAM processes, not for the coarse logic line.
children.note: The distinction: contact/proximity printing needs a full-size mask; a 1:1 projection stepper also prints 1:1 but optically; only a reduction stepper (2x-10x) needs a smaller reticle. Bipolar logic in 1983 was 1:1 by either contact or 1:1 projection. Bipolar logic generally did not use reduction steppers at this node.

children.name: Spinning on the resist
children.description: The wafer is put on a vacuum chuck in a bowl, a few millilitres of resist is dispensed, and the bowl spins at several thousand rpm, flinging the resist into a film of a chosen thickness - thicker where a thick layer is needed to etch deep, thinner where fine resolution is needed. The film is then soft-baked to drive off solvent and stabilise the image.

children.name: The coater/developer track
children.description: A machine with hot plates and spray-heads that automates spin-coat, soft-bake, develop, rinse and bake for a whole cassette of wafers in one pass. The track was the workhorse of the photomask bay: an operator loaded a cassette and pushed a button, and the bay's lithography throughput was set by how many tracks it had.

facts.label: Track throughput
facts.value: ~25 wafers per cycle, ~1 min per cycle

children.note: On a bipolar line in 1983 the resist was still often negative: exposure cross-links the resist so it becomes insoluble in the developer, and the pattern left on the wafer after develop is the complement of the mask. That suits diffusion, where you want to open the mask where the oxide is. Positive resists, which behave the intuitive way, had taken over NMOS and CMOS from the late 1970s but lingered on bipolar. Medium confidence on the specific mix in a given vendor's logic bay: by 1983 positive resists were already dominant for MOS processes (Shipley AZ-1350 and its successors) and the trend across all processes was well advanced, but negative resist on bipolar logic persisted into the 1980s. The chemistry itself - novolac plus photoactive group, alkaline development, image reversal - is published at chem.photoresist and chem.photoresist.negative, which is where the inlined copy of it used to be; both are named in `inputs`.

children.name: Dehydration bake before the resist
children.description: Resist will not stick to a wet wafer, so before every coat the wafer goes on a hot plate or in a dehydration oven at 150-250 C to drive off the adsorbed water from the previous wet step. Skipping it causes the single most common resist defect - the film lifting off in patches during development. Every one of the eight cycles repeats this.

children.name: The dehydration hot plate
children.description: A temperature-controlled aluminium or ceramic plate the cassette sits on for a minute or two at 150-200 C. Cheap, essential, and present at every wet bench in the bay.
children.note: Not established: the plate material, the 150-200 C setpoint, the one or two minute dwell, or that such a plate stood at every wet bench in the bay. A hot plate is a necessary piece of photolithography equipment but no source describes it.

children.name: Aligning the mask to the wafer
children.simple_name: Aligning the mask to the wafer
children.description: The wafer is dried, loaded onto a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and the mask is laid directly on top of it - contact printing - or held just above it with a controlled air gap - proximity printing - or imaged one-to-one through a lens. The machine's job is to align each feature on the mask to the feature already printed on the wafer, usually by optically reading alignment marks etched into the previous level. At 3-5 um, alignment tolerance was generous; at DRAM geometries it was brutal.
children.note: Contact printing was cheapest and fastest but printed mask defects onto every die and wore the mask; proximity printing added an air gap for a small resolution penalty. 1:1 projection steppers (like TI's Micralign, and Perkin-Elmer's) were arriving in the early 1980s and gave a clean image without contact wear. Bipolar logic at 3-5 um was comfortable with any of the three.

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: optical, on marks from previous levels

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: mercury g-line 436 nm or h-line 405 nm

children.name: The contact/proximity mask aligner
children.description: A granite or cast base, a Chuck/Hamble wafer stage with micrometer knobs for theta and X-Y, a vacuum frame to pull the mask down onto the wafer, a mercury lamp below, and a pair of binocular microscopes to watch the alignment marks. One operator could run one or two of these, spending most of the cycle walking up and down the level stack.

children.name: The 1:1 projection stepper
children.description: A mask aligner that images the mask through a fixed 1:1 lens onto the wafer with a small gap, so there is no contact and no wear, and no mask-defect printing. TI's Micralign and Perkin-Elmer's units of the late 1970s and early 1980s brought this to the logic lines. It was the technology that eventually killed contact printing entirely.

children.name: The mercury lamp
children.description: A 1000 W high-pressure mercury arc with a quartz envelope. Its spectrum peaks at 365, 405 and 436 nm; optical filters select one line, almost always 436 nm (g-line) for the finest resolution the era could reach. Newer deep-UV lamps added 248 nm. The lamp is run at constant power because the resist's exposure depends on its intensity, and lamp ageing was a constant yield headache.

children.name: Developing the image
children.description: The exposed wafer is sprayed with an alkaline developer - for a positive resist, a solution of tetramethylammonium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide; for a negative resist, an organic solvent. The unexposed (positive) or exposed (negative) resist dissolves, leaving the pattern in hardened resist. Then a rinse in deionised water, a dry, and a hard-bake to cross-link the remaining resist so it survives the etch that follows. TMAH was preferred because it left no metal ion residues that would poison the device.
children.note: The developer chemistry is named in `inputs` rather than inlined: chem.fab-chemicals.tmah publishes TMAH and its synthesis, and chem.photoresist.development publishes the 0.2-0.3 N spray-development process. A potassium-hydroxide developer, made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine alongside chlorine, was the older alkali and was still in use; the sub-branch that used to sit here (potash -> brine -> rock salt) duplicated metal.salt-brine and metal.chlor-alkali and has been removed.

children.name: Etching the oxide window
children.description: The patterned resist is the stencil; the wafer goes into an etchant. Buffered oxide etch - hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride - attacks the silicon dioxide where the resist is gone, opening the window, and stops at the silicon or at the oxide-nitride beneath. The wafer comes out with resist still on it, which is stripped next. In this era the oxide etch was still wet chemistry; dry plasma etching had not yet replaced it for the bulk oxide.
children.note: Plasma (reactive ion) etching of silicon dioxide was introduced in the early-to-mid 1980s and became standard later in the decade; a 1983 bipolar logic line used wet HF and BOE for its diffusion and contact windows. Hydrofluoric acid, the buffered-etch process and the fluorspar it is made from are named in `inputs` (chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid and its buffered-hf and fluorspar children); the fluorspar-to-HF chain, including the Derbyshire, Ilkley, Mexican, South African and Chinese fluorspar fields and the limestone by-product, used to be inlined beneath this node and is published at metal.fluorspar.

facts.label: Selectivity
facts.value: etches SiO2, stops at Si and Si3N4

children.name: Stripping the resist
children.description: With the etch done, the resist has served its purpose and is removed. In this era, because resist was often negative and organic, a chlorinated solvent strip in a hot bath was standard - historically xylene, then trichloroethylene, boiling at 87 C. Solvent stripping leaves ionic residue, which had to be followed by a piranha clean, a rinse, and a dehydration bake before the next coat. Trichloroethylene was ubiquitous as a resist strip and a vapour degreaser in this period and was being phased out for toxicity and ozone reasons through the 1980s, replaced by perchloroethylene and then by piranha wet strips.
children.note: That the resist is removed after etch by dry stripping or plasma ashing or by a wet resist stripper is documented. Not established: chlorinated solvents as the standard route, the xylene-then-trichloroethylene sequence, the 87 C boiling point, the piranha wet strip, and the phasing out of trichloroethylene through the 1980s.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.name: The junction-isolated bipolar flow
mb.logic.bipolar.process.description: The sequence that turns a plain slice of silicon into a chip of interconnected bipolar transistors. Four diffusion cycles do all the work: an n+ isolation diffusion to separate each transistor into its own island; a p base diffusion under the island to form the transistor base; an n+ emitter diffusion into the base to form the emitter; and the Schottky-barrier levels that give the 'LS' in 74LS its name. Between and inside those cycles sit an epitaxial growth, a thin-film resistor deposition, a metallisation and a passivation.

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: n+ phosphorus, driven to the substrate

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: n+ phosphorus or arsenic, Rs ~10-30 ohm/sq

children.name: Epitaxial growth of the collector
children.description: The single most distinctive step of the bipolar process. The wafer is placed in a horizontal reactor and a few micrometres of lightly doped n-type silicon is grown on top of it in a hydrogen atmosphere at about 1100-1200 C. The growing layer inherits the crystal lattice of the wafer below, so the n-type collector sits on the p-type substrate as a perfect single crystal - a vertical diode. Without epi, a vertical bipolar transistor would be impossible.
children.note: The reactor also dopes: phosphine or arsine is mixed into the hydrogen stream so the epilayer comes out n-type to a controlled resistivity. This is one of only two places (the other being the isolation and emitter diffusions) where a distinct dopant chemistry is needed. The gas box fed silane or trichlorosilane in dry, ultra-pure hydrogen - not trichloroethylene, which is a degreasing solvent and not an epitaxial source, and not hydrogen chloride. Silicon tetrachloride was the older, hotter source. The dopant gases themselves are named in `inputs` and published at chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.

children.name: The horizontal epitaxial reactor
children.description: A quartz or silicon-carbide tube with a graphite susceptor that is heated by a radio-frequency induction coil. Silane or trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow past; the silicon atoms deposit on the hot wafer. Inductors rotate the wafer and provide the radiant heat. Loaded by hand or by a cassette elevator; a batch of 20-30 wafers takes an hour or two.
children.note: Not established: the quartz or silicon-carbide tube, the graphite susceptor, the radio-frequency induction coil, the 1000-2000 W coupling, the 20-30 wafer batch or the one to two hour cycle. Epitaxial growth in a vapour phase is documented; this reactor description is not.

children.name: Growth of the field oxide
children.description: Silicon dioxide grown by passing steam over the wafer at 900-1050 C. This thick oxide is the field oxide: it covers everything except the windows that are later cut for diffusion and metallisation, and it is what electrically and physically isolates one transistor island from the next, in the same way the oxide isolates a MOS gate.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: mask for diffusion + isolation + field-effect control

children.name: The oxidation furnace
children.description: A horizontal tube furnace, quartz or silicon-carbide, heated to 1000 C, with wet oxygen or steam flowing through. The wafer rides on a quartz boat pushed in and out by a loader. Oxidation is the slowest step in a bipolar line and the furnaces are the bottleneck.

children.name: Collector-collector isolation
children.description: The first diffusion. Where the field oxide has windows, phosphorus is driven in to make a heavily n-doped region that runs all the way down to the p-type substrate. Everything inside a window is now n-type; the n+ walls around and between windows cut the wafer into separate n-type islands, each with a p substrate beneath it. Two n+ islands separated by a p-substrate region form back-to-back diodes, and those diodes are the isolation - a device made entirely of unwanted junctions doing an essential job.
children.note: The isolation junctions carry the full supply voltage between adjacent islands, so they are reverse-biased diodes and must be kept clean and leak-free. Guard rings and careful gettering protect them.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: through the n-epilayer into the substrate

children.name: Diffusion into the window
children.description: The wafer is coated with a phosphorus-bearing dopant source - a spun-on emulsion or a deposited glass - then pushed into a furnace at 1000-1150 C. Heat alone moves the phosphorus atoms down into the silicon, opening up and closing the junction as it goes. Diffusion, not implantation, because diffusion gives the smooth graded junctions that give a transistor its gain.

children.name: Guard rings around the islands
children.description: A ring of n+ material, often tied to the most positive supply, laid around each sensitive island. It intercepts stray minority carriers and surface charge before they can reach the isolation junction, and it raises the breakdown voltage of the isolation. Guard rings are one of the oldest tricks in the planar process and were still drawn on a 1983 logic layout.

children.name: What a guard ring physically is
children.description: Not a new material - just the same n+ diffusion, but drawn as a closed loop around the transistor instead of a small dot. The mask for the isolation diffusion draws the guard ring at the same time as the island, so it costs one more shape on one mask and no extra process step. That is the whole elegance of it.
children.note: Not established: that a guard ring is the same diffusion drawn as a closed loop at no extra process step, and therefore free at the mask level. The guard ring itself is undocumented in the sources available, so this description of it is too.

Not established by any source available. There is no encyclopaedia article on the semiconductor guard ring - the article of that name is about driven guards in thyristors - and the minor-carrier collection and breakdown-voltage claims are not in any handbook text reached here.

children.name: Dielectric isolation (Fairchild's alternative)
children.description: Instead of relying on reverse-biased isolation diodes, the islands can be sunk into a solid thermally grown oxide so each is completely surrounded by insulating oxide. The wafer is oxidised, then diffusion (or epitaxy) is done into small windows in the oxide; the oxide under the silicon is never removed, so no vertical isolation junction exists at all. This gives lower capacitance and better speed but is much harder to make, because the silicon has to be grown in a hole in oxide without lifting it.
children.note: Dielectric isolation was used by Fairchild and a few others for high-performance analog and for some logic families in the 1970s and 1980s, but junction isolation was cheaper and dominated standard 74LS. Not established: which isolation a given vendor's 74LS used; most 74LS parts are believed to be junction-isolated. The citation that used to sit here, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dielectric_isolation, does not exist: there is no encyclopaedia article on dielectric isolation of bipolar circuits, and the plausible nearby subjects are about something else (isolation transformers, through-silicon vias, dielectric withstand testing). It was removed rather than repointed at a misleading neighbour, so nothing here rests on a link a reader can follow.

children.name: Deep trench isolation (later, and now extinct in logic)
children.description: For the highest-performance bipolar processes - the ones behind linear amplifiers and the last power logic - isolation was cut as a deep trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide or polysilicon, then buried. This gives near-vertical isolation walls and far lower capacitance than the lateral isolation diffusion. It was expensive and it is now essentially extinct in merchant logic.
children.note: The brief asked for the deep-trench-isolation-came-later point. Confirmed: trench isolation appeared in high-performance bipolar through the 1980s and 1990s and is gone from the logic business entirely, because CMOS with shallow-trench isolation simply won.

children.name: The base diffusion
children.description: A second diffusion. Through a new mask, boron is driven into each n-island to make the p-type base of the transistor. The base is the thinnest and most tightly controlled region in the whole structure - roughly half to one micrometre deep - because the transistor's gain and its maximum speed both come from how narrow the base is. Every minute the base is too wide, the transistor is slow.

facts.label: Why thin
facts.value: base transit time sets transistor fT

children.name: The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it
children.description: The third diffusion. Through a finer mask, a very heavily doped n+ region is driven into the boron base, forming the emitter. Because the n+ emitter is so much more heavily doped than the p base, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased at only 0.7 V and injects enormous current gain - but only as long as the emitter does not punch through the thin base under the reverse bias of the collector. Pushing gold into the emitter diffuses the emitter junction forward slightly, making the junction harder for holes to reverse-inject, which suppresses punch-through and the associated capacitance, and raises the gain. This is the 'gold-doped emitter'.
children.note: The gold-doped (Au-doped) polysilicon emitter was a real and important technique of this era, used to raise gain and suppress the emitter-base reverse conductance ('knee'). It was implemented by co-depositing a tiny amount of gold in the emitter polysilicon or dopant glass, then driving it in with the arsenic or phosphorus. Confidence medium: the technique is well documented, but it is not confirmed that a specific 74LS vendor's 1983 process used it; it was common in high-performance bipolar rather than mandatory in low-cost logic. A self-aligned polysilicon emitter - deposit a thin arsenic-doped polysilicon film, pattern it to define the emitter, then push, so the arsenic is confined by the polysilicon walls and the emitter comes out shallower and more uniform - was the other refinement of the era, widespread in analog through the 1980s and 1990s and doubtful on a commodity 74LS. The arsine itself is an ingredient and is named in `inputs`, not inlined as a child; its provenance is worth recording: arsenic occurs as arsenide in copper and lead concentrates, roasting drives it off as arsenic trioxide fume, and the trioxide is reduced and hydrogenated to arsine. Arsenic-bearing copper concentrates were a notorious long-time smelting hazard, which is why arsenic control in copper works is a regulated topic today.

facts.label: Gold purpose
facts.value: suppress emitter-base reverse leakage and push-through

children.name: The Schottky clamp - the S in LS
children.simple_name: Schottky clamp, the S in LS
children.description: In standard 7400-series TTL a transistor saturates when it is driven hard: both junctions forward-biased, charge stored in the base, and the transistor slow to turn off. A 74LS puts a small Schottky diode - metal to lightly doped n-type, with no forward drop - from each transistor's base to its collector. When the base tries to go more forward than a silicon junction would allow, the Schottky diode conducts first and steals the excess, pinning the collector voltage just above saturation. The transistor never saturates, so it turns off in a couple of nanoseconds instead of twenty. That is the whole 'Schottky' idea, and it is why an LS gate is fast and still low-power.
children.note: The Schottky barrier itself is formed simply by touching aluminium to the lightly doped n-type collector (aluminium-silicon is 0.75 eV work-function difference against n-Si) - no extra mask beyond the one that defines the collector contact, because the Schottky diode and the ohmic collector contact are made in the same window. So the LS family costs the same number of mask levels as plain TTL. First commercial Schottky TTL was TI's 74S series, 1964.

facts.label: Barrier
facts.value: Al on n-type Si, ~0.75 eV work-function difference

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: prevents transistor saturation; 74LS gate delay ~10 ns

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: no extra mask - same window as the collector contact

children.name: The NiCr thin-film resistor level
children.description: A 74LS is full of resistors - the pull-ups, the current-limiting elements, the bias network. On a junction-isolated bipolar logic line they were made as a deposited thin film of nickel-chromium alloy, sputtered onto the wafer, patterned by one extra mask, and annealed. This is the one mask level that separates the 74LS flow from a plainer bipolar analog flow, and it is why an 'LS' logic wafer and an analog bipolar wafer had different mask counts.
children.note: Resistors in this class were 'thin film', not 'thick film': the NiCr was deposited in a vacuum (sputtered) to a controlled sheet resistance of order 100-250 ohm/square, then laser- or acid-trimmed to value. Low-power TTL needed relatively low resistances, so a common sheet resistance was fine. Precision analog parts moved to laser trimming and, later, to scaled 'valley' resistors.

facts.label: Trimming
facts.value: laser trim for precision; as-deposited for logic

children.name: The RF/DC sputterer
children.description: A vacuum chamber pumped to a low argon pressure, a cathode holding the NiCr target, the wafer as the anode. An RF or DC glow discharge strikes the target, argon ions knock nickel and chromium atoms loose, and they deposit onto the wafer. It is a slow, line-of-sight, unidirectional process - which is why sputtered NiCr resistors are behind the same shadow problems as sputtered metal interconnect.

children.name: The contact window
children.description: One more mask, which cuts small windows in the field oxide wherever a metal film needs to reach the silicon underneath - the collector, the base, the emitter. Each window is a hole a few micrometres across. The oxide elsewhere is untouched, and it is the oxide that keeps the aluminium from shorting to the substrate everywhere except where you wanted it to.

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: HF through the oxide to the silicon

children.name: Aluminium metallisation
children.description: The final mask. A layer of aluminium about 1 micrometre thick is deposited over the whole wafer - sputtered or evaporated - and a mask removes it everywhere except the wires. Those wires connect the transistor terminals, the resistors, and the bonding pads around the edge of the die. One single metal level, no vias, no second layer. This is the single biggest reason a 1983 logic chip was so simple to make: routing was almost free because the cells were small.
children.note: That physical vapour deposition was the primary deposition technique until chemical vapour deposition took over in the 1980s is documented. Not established: the 1-1.5 um film thickness, the single-level, no-via constraint, or the comparison that bipolar needed two or three metal layers once it shrank.

children.name: Sintering the metal into the contacts
children.description: After aluminium is deposited, the wafer is pushed briefly to 400-450 C in hydrogen or forming gas. This melts the aluminium into the contact windows, welding it to the silicon and lowering the contact resistance, and it anneals out the sputter damage in the silicon. It is a short, cheap step and it is the reason the metallisation recipe ends with a hydrogen firing.
children.note: Aluminium sintering / hydrogen alloying at 400-450 C was standard in the era. Confidence medium on the exact temperature window; the purpose and the technique are not in doubt. The forming gas is an ingredient: nitrogen and hydrogen are named in `inputs`, not hung off as children, because a gas supply line is not part of a wafer.

children.name: Passivation over the metal
children.description: A final film - silicon dioxide, usually with a nitride cap - deposited over the finished aluminium, opened again only at the bonding pads and along the scribe lanes. It seals the chip against moisture and mobile ions, which is what lets a 1983 logic part hold a 15-year life in a consumer television.

mb.logic.cmos.litho.name: The photolithography is the same, but the resist is positive
mb.logic.cmos.litho.description: A CMOS line of 1983 reused the same mask aligners, coaters and developers as the bipolar line next door. The one substantive difference is the resist: by the end of the 1970s the NMOS and CMOS lines had already switched to positive resists such as Shipley's AZ-1350, while bipolar logic was still often running negative resists. Positive resists tolerate the small misalignment that LOCOS bird's-beak and oxide steps cause better, which is part of why MOS won.
mb.logic.cmos.litho.note: The positive-resist chemistry - a novolac resin with a photosensitive protecting group, exposure breaking the group off so the exposed resin becomes soluble in alkaline developer, the pattern on the wafer taking the same polarity as the pattern on the mask - is not inlined here; chem.photoresist publishes it and is named in `inputs`. Positive resists went from invention in the 1940s to default in the late 1970s, had won MOS by 1983, and were displacing negative resist on bipolar; within a decade negative resist was gone from production lines entirely.

facts.label: Adoption
facts.value: NMOS from the late 1970s; all production lines by the early 1990s

mb.logic.cmos.process.name: The twin-tub CMOS flow
mb.logic.cmos.process.description: The order of a CMOS process is dictated by one rule: you can never put anything back into silicon after a high-temperature step, so everything that must survive later furnace work is done first, in descending order of temperature. Wells, then field oxide, then thin gate oxide, then polysilicon, then the self-aligned source/drain implants at a low temperature, then metal.

children.name: n-well and p-well implants
children.description: Two masked implants. Phosphorus (or arsenic) goes into the n-well; boron into the p-well. At 3-5 um these were thermal diffusions or, increasingly, implantations - by the early 1980s medium-current implanters were displacing diffusion in CMOS, the opposite trend to bipolar, where diffusion survived much longer. An implantation is done cold and fast: the dopant is accelerated into the surface at tens of keV and stops almost where it is put.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: ion implantation (thermal diffusion still in use)

children.name: The medium-current ion implanter
children.description: A big steel vacuum chamber with a source, an analysing magnet, an accelerating column and a beamline down to a scan platter that holds the wafer. The dopant is ionised, selected by mass, accelerated to tens of keV, and swept across the wafer. Implanters were expensive, and CMOS was the process that made them a standard line tool rather than a special one.
children.note: Implanters were standard in CMOS lines by the early 1980s; diffusion was still the workhorse in bipolar logic, which is one of the more interesting differences between the two processes. The dopant gases are the same three the bipolar line uses - phosphine for the n-well, diborane for the p-well, sometimes arsine - and they are ingredients named in `inputs`, published once at chem.fab-chemicals.dopants. Electricity is a cross-cutting service and is a `from` edge, not a component.

children.name: LOCOS isolation
children.description: Locally Oxidised Silicon. Where two transistors must not touch, the field oxide is simply grown. A layer of silicon nitride is deposited and patterned; the wafer is oxidised in steam, so oxide grows everywhere the nitride is absent; the nitride is stripped off in hot phosphoric acid, leaving a thick field oxide behind. It is isolation by oxidising rather than by doping, and it is the reason a CMOS chip looks like a quilt of raised oxide platforms.

facts.label: Mask oxide
facts.value: Si3N4, LPCVD from silane and ammonia

facts.label: Known problem
facts.value: the 'bird's beak' - the field oxide grows sideways and eats into the active area

children.name: The gate oxide
children.description: Inside the active windows the thin gate oxide is grown, by dry oxidation in oxygen at about 1000 C. On a 3-5 um part it is 80-120 nm thick - a few hundred atom layers. This film is the transistor: its thickness sets the threshold voltage and its capacitance sets the drive current, and it is the thinnest and most fragile thing on the chip. At 1983's feature sizes it was still thick by modern standards, which is one reason CMOS of that era was not yet faster than bipolar.

children.name: The polysilicon gate
children.description: A layer of polycrystalline silicon is deposited over the whole wafer, then doped (usually with phosphorus from phosphine, or with POCL3 in a furnace) so that it conducts, then patterned. That patterned polysilicon is the gate. Crucially, it is also used as the mask for the source and drain implant immediately afterwards - so the gate aligns itself, and no extra mask is needed. The self-aligned gate and source/drain, invented at Fairchild in the late 1960s, is the single idea that made CMOS manufacturable at all.
children.note: The silane feed is SiH4, decomposing on a hot surface at 700-850 C to lay down pure polycrystalline silicon - cleaner and more controllable than trichlorosilane because it carries no chlorine and no corrosive by-products. Trichlorosilane still dominated for boule-grade silicon. A 4000-series part might also deposit a few resistors from this same film: polysilicon resistors cost nothing extra because they are made at the same time as the gate, from the same film, at no extra mask. That the 4066 specifically uses on-chip polysilicon resistors is plausible from its trim and bias requirements but is not verified against a cross-section, and some 4000-series parts use no resistors at all.

facts.label: Doping
facts.value: phosphine in the deposition, or POCL3 furnace

children.name: The self-aligned source and drain
children.description: With the gate already patterned in polysilicon, the source and drain are implanted straight through the exposed silicon beside it, and the gate itself blocks the implant everywhere it is. No alignment mask is needed: the gate defines the gap between source and drain by its own edge. Two implants, phosphorus for the n-channel source/drain and boron for the p-channel, each masked by the opposite field oxide. This is 'self-aligned', and it is the reason a CMOS transistor's channel length is set by a printed line width and nothing else.

facts.label: Masking
facts.value: the polysilicon gate itself, plus the opposite field oxide

children.note: That boron and phosphorus are the p- and n-type dopants and that implantation is followed by an activation anneal is documented. Not established: that the source and drain were self-aligned to a polysilicon gate on this part, or the 0.2-0.5 um junction depth. The self-alignment mechanism is not described in the sources available.

children.name: The source/drain anneal
children.description: After the implant the wafer goes back into a furnace briefly to heal the crystal damage and to activate the dopant atoms into substitutional positions. This is the one remaining high-temperature step, and it is why CMOS still used a furnace in the era when bipolar was moving to implantation.
children.note: The activation anneal was around 800-900 C for an hour, or a rapid thermal anneal of a few seconds at 1000 C plus. Medium confidence on the exact numbers.

children.name: Contact and aluminium interconnect
children.description: The field oxide is etched away over the source, drain and gate to expose silicon, then aluminium is deposited and patterned into one single layer of interconnect. Exactly the same metallisation as the bipolar line, exactly the same problems (step coverage over the oxide steps, electromigration under current) and exactly the same solution in this era: one level, because at 3-5 um the cells were big enough to route around with a single layer.
children.note: Not established: the etch that opens the contact, the single aluminium level, the step-coverage and electromigration problems, or the claim that one level sufficed because the cells were large. Aluminium as the 1980s wiring metal and the later move to copper are documented in general; the level count for a 1983 4000-series part is not.

children.name: Passivation, and why CMOS needed less of it
children.description: An interlayer oxide and a final nitride cap, opened only at the pads and scribe lanes. A CMOS device is far less sensitive to mobile ions than a bipolar one, because a CMOS gate draws no gate current and its threshold is set electrostatically rather than by charge state; so the passivation job is easier and the nitride does most of the work.
children.note: The relative immunity of CMOS to mobile charge is standard device physics; the specific passivation stack comparison is a reasonable generalisation rather than a cited measurement.

mb.logic.package.assembly.name: Die attach, wire bond, moulding
mb.logic.package.assembly.description: Three operations turn a loose die and a loose lead frame into a component. The die is brazed to the frame's central ledge. Twenty-ish gold wires are ball- or wedge-bonded from pads on the die to the inner ends of the pins. Then about 0.3-0.5 g of filled black epoxy is transfer-moulded over everything and cured.

children.name: Die attach to the frame paddle
children.simple_name: Die attach to the frame paddle
children.description: The die is placed face-down onto a small ledge in the middle of the lead frame and brazed there with a preform of gold-silicon eutectic at 350-400 C. The eutectic melts before the silicon itself does, so the joint is made without heating the chip to a temperature that would damage it. Cheap parts instead used a silver-filled organic paste cured on a hot plate, or conductive epoxy, and some logic used glass-frit die attach for thermal cycling.
children.note: Organic die attach became common in the late 1980s-90s for cost reasons. In 1983 Au-Si eutectic brazing was still the standard on logic and memory.

children.name: Gold wire bonding
children.description: A machine called a wedge bonder presses a hair-thin gold wire onto an aluminium bonding pad with a tungsten or ceramic tool while a hydrogen torch or arc welds them together, then repeats at the inner end of the pin. Each joint is a small aluminium-gold intermetallic wedge, and the wire is parted by tearing it rather than by cutting it. It is the cheapest way ever devised to connect a chip to the outside world, and it is why every 1983 logic chip has that characteristic fan of gold legs.
children.note: Ball bonding, with a 2.5 mil wire and ~25-50 bonds per second, was displacing wedge bonding for high pin counts in this period. Wedge bonding at ~10 bonds per second dominated merchant logic.

children.name: The wedge bonder
children.description: A two-station machine that draws wire from a spool, forms a loop, drives a wedge onto the die pad under a hydrogen flame, swings 90 degrees, and drives the second wedge onto the pin, then snaps the wire. Twenty or forty of these sat in a row along a packaging line, each attended by one operator feeding frames in and taking packaged parts out.

children.name: Transfer moulding the black epoxy body
children.description: A slab of thermosetting epoxy loaded with 75-85 percent spherical silica is melted at 175 C and forced through a small orifice into a multi-cavity steel mould - the transfer mould - that holds the wired frame in one cavity per die. The compound flows around the wire loops, fills voids, and cures in three to five minutes. Because it is filled with silica it is not really a plastic in the loose sense: it is a ceramic-filled thermoset whose job is to hold the die in place, carry heat away, and keep moisture out. Moulding compounds are incompletely polymerised at the mould temperature, so the parts are then baked for hours at 175 C to complete the cure and drive off the last of the residual stress - a batch operation, thousands of parts in a tray, on a schedule that ran overnight.
children.note: The post-mould stability bake: thousands of parts in a tray, overnight, completing a cure that the mould itself cannot finish.

facts.label: Post-mould bake
facts.value: 175 C for 4-24 h - completes cure and moisture equilibration

children.name: The transfer press
children.description: A heated platen press with a pot and plunger that transfers melted compound into the mould. Modern machines are multi-cavity and run at thousands of shots an hour; a 1980s line used 20- to 100-shot multi-cavity tools and got through a few hundred thousand DIPs a month.
children.note: Capital equipment, so a tool rather than a part.

children.name: The mould cavity and ejector pins
children.description: A hardened, polished steel block with one to hundreds of identical cavities. For a DIP the cavity is a rectangle with fourteen to twenty pin-shaped slots; the mould also carries the moulded cavity number, the vendor's part-number embossing, and ejector pins that push the finished part out without scuffing it. Moulds lasted a few hundred thousand to a few million shots.
children.note: A consumable tool, not a machine: it is bought, used up over its shot life and thrown away, so `part` rather than `tool`. Its earlier `inputs: [metal.silica]` was wrong - nothing in a hardened steel mould is silica - and has been removed.

facts.label: Cavity marks
facts.value: the number 1 or a letter, moulded into the underside

mb.logic.package.marking.name: Marking the top of the package
mb.logic.package.marking.description: Ink printing was still the norm in 1983: a pad or a dot-matrix printer lays the part number, the manufacturer's mark, a date code (year and week, e.g. 8341) and a lot or assembly code on the moulded surface. Laser marking was beginning to appear, mostly for military parts, and would take over within a decade because a laser-marked part cannot be relabelled.
mb.logic.package.marking.note: Commodore bought these chips from several vendors and did not re-mark them, which is why an original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore house number, all mixed together. Laser marking - a Q-switched Nd:YAG or CO2 laser ablating characters into the epoxy surface, or a carbon laser removing the top layer to expose an underlying white layer - was indelible and fast but in 1983 was still a premium option used mostly for military marking, adopted more widely through the mid-to-late 1980s.

facts.label: Packaging of record
facts.value: tubed, then later dry-packed and taped

mb.logic.package.probe.name: Probe test before packaging
mb.logic.package.probe.description: Die that fail are thrown away before they are worth a lead frame. The wafer is loaded onto a probe stage, a probe card with one needle per bonding pad is lowered onto it, and a tester runs every pattern and every DC parameter. Only known-good die are cut. This is why probe test and not final test is what sets the economics of a logic wafer: a yield loss after packaging has already cost you the moulding and the wire bonds too.

children.name: The wafer probe station
children.description: A heavy cast stage that steps the wafer die by die under a fixed probe card: a vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, a microscope to line the card up, and a needle interface to the tester. An operator loads a cassette of up to 25 wafers and unloads it at the end; everything in between was automatic.
children.note: Not established: the cast stage, the vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, the 25-wafer cassette, the 1-4 die per second probing speed or the 20-80 g per needle contact force. No prober specification is in any source available.

children.name: The logic tester
children.description: An automated test system running a stored functional pattern and a set of DC limit tests per device type: propagation delay, fan-out current, input current, output high and low voltage, and the truth table at the functional corners. A 74LS04 has a few hundred such tests. The tester was the expensive part of probe test and was amortised across every device type on the line.
children.note: Automatic test equipment: capital equipment shared across every device type on the line, so a tool rather than a part or a consumable.

facts.label: Instrumentation
facts.value: TTL pattern generator, timing analyser, DC meter

mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.name: Glass frit sealing
mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.description: A paste of powdered borosilicate glass with a small amount of binder is applied around the rim, the lid is set on it, and the assembly goes through a sealing furnace. The glass melts, wets the metallised ceramic and the metal lid, and on cooling forms a hermetic, dimensionally matched bond. The temperature profile - ramp, soak around 700-750 C, controlled cool - is the whole art of it.
mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.note: Sealing in a continuous belt or pusher furnace at a few hundred degrees per hour rather than 700-750 C soak is the classic profile; the exact numbers vary by package. Medium confidence on the peak temperature.

mb.logic.package.die.passivation.name: The glass over the aluminium
mb.logic.package.die.passivation.description: After metallisation the whole wafer is coated in a thick film of silicon dioxide, usually with a plasma-deposited nitride cap. This passivation layer is what protects a 1983 logic die from the humidity and mobile ions that would otherwise creep under the aluminium and shift the threshold of a transistor. Openings in it are the bonding pads and the scribe lanes.
mb.logic.package.die.passivation.note: Early 1980s nitride deposition was increasingly low-pressure or plasma-enhanced CVD from silane and ammonia; furnaces using TEOS plus ammonia still ran in parallel.

mb.logic.package.die.scribe.name: Scribing and dicing the wafer
mb.logic.package.die.scribe.description: A diamond stylus is dragged along the scribe lanes between dies, not to cut through but to fracture the crystal along the damage tracks buried in the oxide. For the narrow lanes the wafer is turned edge-on and run through a rotating diamond blade, or more recently a tensioned wire loaded with abrasive, which leaves far less chipping than a blade.
mb.logic.package.die.scribe.note: The diamond itself - natural or, by 1983, mostly synthetic grit from graphite in a belt press (si.wafer.diamond.grit, contained in scriber/saw blades) - is used via tools, not taken in as a process feedstock; scribe uses diamond tools.

facts.label: Blade kerf
facts.value: ~0.15 mm for a resinoid dicing saw

mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.name: Lead plating: tin, gold flash, nickel
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.description: Bare nickel-iron leads solder badly and gall when the DIP is pushed into and out of a socket, so every logic lead frame came out of the stamping press already plated. The common 1983 finish was an electroless or electrolytic nickel pre-plate followed by a matte tin or tin-lead overlay; gold flash over nickel was used where a part had to survive many insertions. A small fraction of frames used silver.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.note: Matte tin plating on lead frames later became a reliability problem - tin whiskers - and the industry spent two decades fixing it. Copper-clad (C4) frames that carry a thicker, more solderable surface metal appeared in the late 1980s and 1990s, which is why the C64's successors used them and the C64 did not.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.name: Progressive-die stamping of the frame
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.description: The strip is fed through a sequence of steel dies on a mechanical press. Each station cuts, pierces, forms and bends a little more; by the last station the strip has a repeating row of completed DIP skeletons still joined by their tie bars. Ten to twenty tonnes of press capacity for a strip that is a tenth of a millimetre thick and has to be dimensioned to a few microns.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.note: Photo-etched lead frames from copper and copper alloys were an alternative for high-lead-count parts, but the stamping route dominated through-hole logic DIPs in this period.

facts.label: Tie bars
facts.value: left until after the die is attached, to hold the frame rigid

children.name: The progressive die set
children.description: A stack of hardened tool-steel plates, each with apertures and forming punches cut by wire EDM or grinding, bolted into a set between the press bolster and the ram. Making the tooling for one frame number was a days-to-weeks job and was why a lead frame number was never changed casually: the tooling, the mould, the socket and the board artwork all had to change together.
children.note: A press toolset, consumed over hundreds of millions of strokes - capital equipment rather than a part.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.name: The mask writer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.description: A computer-controlled plotter that draws the pattern onto the chrome layer - a direct-write electron-beam or laser writer, or a mask stepper using photographic reduction for the simpler logic geometries. The mask set for one part number was the output of days of the mask shop's finest-resolution tool, and it was checked by eye under a microscope before use.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.note: For 3-5 um logic geometries, a photographic mask stepper was adequate and much faster than electron-beam writing; beam writing was reserved for the DRAM and custom-chip masks.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.name: Boron as the p dopant
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.description: Boron, the p-type dopant, came either as diborane gas or as a thin boron-doped oxide or boron nitride wafer, and was the standard acceptor for base diffusions throughout the era. It is an ingredient of the diffusion, so it hangs off `inputs` (chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane) rather than as a child.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.name: The gold in the emitter
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.description: A fraction of a percent of gold, introduced by co-doping the emitter source and driven in with the emitter diffusion. Gold is a deep acceptor-diffusing substitutional impurity in silicon; it behaves in the base like a recombination centre. In the emitter-base junction it forward-shifts the junction for electrons and suppresses hole injection into the emitter, which is what raises gain and kills the reverse gain of the transistor.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.note: Gold as a recombination centre in silicon is well established physics; its use in Au-doped emitters is a documented period technique. Exact concentration is on the order of a fraction of a percent in the emitter. metal.gold is an ingredient, so it hangs off `inputs`.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.name: The nickel-chromium sputtering target
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.description: A block of 80/20 nickel-chromium alloy that the sputter gun erodes. High-purity nickel and chromium are the two metals that dominate this one thin film; the chromium is what gives the film its near-zero temperature coefficient, and the nickel is what makes it resistive rather than metallic.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.note: Nickel and chromium are ingredients of the film, so they hang off `inputs` (metal.nickel, metal.chromium) rather than as children.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quart.name: Fused quartz tube and boat
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quart.description: The tube the wafer sits in is fused quartz, because quartz holds up to about 1100 C and is chemically inert to the oxidising atmosphere. Quartz is itself manufactured from high-purity silicon, so the tube and the silicon it processes came from related chemistry.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.name: Deionised process steam
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.description: Ultra-pure water turned to vapour in the furnace inlet. The water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold. Fab water came from municipal supply through a chain of reverse osmosis and ion exchange. Steam is an ingredient of the oxidation step, not a component of the furnace, so it hangs off `inputs` rather than as a child.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.note: Deionised steam, fed to the furnace inlet: the water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold.

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.name: The silicon nitride masking film
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.description: A layer of amorphous silicon nitride, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition from silane and ammonia at about 800 C. It is used in three places in a CMOS line: as the mask that protects active areas during field oxidation, as the encapsulant under the nitride passivation at the end, and as a spacer. Nitride is chosen because it is immune to hot steam - which is precisely why it is a good mask for something that is about to be steamed. Its two feed gases are named in `inputs`: monosilane (chem.silane.monosilane) for the silicon, and electronic-grade ammonia (chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide, delivered as anhydrous NH3 sparged into ultrapure water) for the nitrogen. In 1983 essentially all industrial ammonia was made by Haber-Bosch - nitrogen from the air plus hydrogen from steam-reformed natural gas over an iron catalyst at 400-500 C and 200-300 atm - so the film that defines a CMOS transistor's isolation runs, indirectly, on natural gas.
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.note: The ammonia sub-branch that used to sit here - ammonia, the nitrogen from the air, the hydrogen from the reformer - duplicated chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide, facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air and chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen, and has been removed. Monosilane and ammonium hydroxide are ingredients, so they hang off `inputs`.

facts.label: Ammonia route
facts.value: Haber-Bosch from air nitrogen and steam-reformed hydrogen, ~450 C, 200-300 atm

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.name: Hot phosphoric acid
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.description: Silicon nitride is attacked by hot concentrated phosphoric acid and by nothing else practical, so a boiling phosphoric acid bath is the standard way to remove it - which is why LOCOS needs an acid tank that no other step in the line does. The acid was made by burning phosphorus, itself from phosphate rock, in excess air and absorbing the oxide in water.
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.note: The chemistry is high confidence; the specific tank temperature (~150-180 C) is a standard process figure but is not verified against a 1983 datasheet.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Epoxy moulding compound
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: A blend of roughly 15-20 percent resin system and 80-85 percent filler by weight. The resin is an epoxy-novolac cured by a phenolic novolac; the filler is spherical fused or precipitated silica graded from a few microns up to about 100 microns so the compound can be both thin enough to flow around a 25 um wire and stiff enough to survive handling; and there is a trace of carbon black pigment to make the part black, plus a trace of mould release. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s.

facts.label: Resin system
facts.value: epoxy cresol novolac + phenolic novolac hardener

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: The silica filler is an ingredient, not a component, so it hangs off `inputs` (metal.silica, metal.quartzite) rather than as a child. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s. The resin and the pigment really are constituents of the compound, so those two stay as children; everything the resin is itself made from is an ingredient of the resin, one level down.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.name: Tin plating bath
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.description: A chemical or electrolytic tin deposit, typically 1-3 micrometres thick, over a nickel underlayer. Tin is soft, wets solder readily and costs almost nothing, and it is why a logic chip could be soldered onto a two-layer board with a plain iron in an automated wave-solder machine with no special flux. The refined tin came from cassiterite smelted in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand or Bolivia.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.note: The name is kept as-is because two nodes in the silicon fragment resolve their 'tin plating bath' ingredient to this id by name; renaming it would silently break those edges and the repoint is proposed rather than applied. The deeper tin chemistry - cassiterite, the Southeast Asian belt and the 1985-86 International Tin Council price collapse - is not inlined here: metal.cassiterite and metal.tin publish it. The general plating process for steel and copper alloys is metal.tin.plating.

mb.logic.package.marking.ink.name: Marking ink
mb.logic.package.marking.ink.description: A phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, laid on and baked, or cured by UV. Cheap and utterly routine - but it is why an original C64 chip is still readable today and a modern BGA is not. (Ink marking was also curable by laser ablation of the mould compound, which is the mechanism the laser marking route exploits.)
mb.logic.package.marking.ink.note: That the legend is printed in ink or by laser and carries a four-digit year-and-week date code is documented. Not established: a phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, baking or UV curing, or that ink marking is why a 1982 part is still readable and a modern ball-grid array is not.

org.philips.name: Philips (N.V. Philips)
org.philips.description: Dutch electronics group; owner of Signetics since 1975 (per the Signetics node note). Created Wave 4 as the documented parent for the Signetics owned-by link.
org.philips.note: Low confidence beyond the ownership fact carried from mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics.

mb.logic.package.probe.card.name: The probe card
mb.logic.package.probe.card.description: A ceramic or printed-circuit substrate carrying one cantilever needle per bonding pad, cantilevered down from an epoxy or quartz shell so the needles survive hundreds of thousands of touches on hard silicon. Building a card for a new part number took days and cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, which is why a device that sold for thirty cents could not afford a new probe card per variant.
mb.logic.package.probe.card.note: Not established: the ceramic or printed-circuit card substrate, the cantilever needle construction, the needle lifetime in touches, or the days and hundreds-to-thousands of dollars to build a card for a new part number. Wafer test before dicing is documented; the card is not.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.name: Texas Instruments
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.description: The company that invented the 7400 series in 1964 and the Schottky TTL in 1964-65, and the largest supplier of the 74LS catalogue. It ran its own fabs (among them Dallas, Sugar Land in Texas, and Niceville in Florida) and also did foundry work for others - the fab-forum business was a real cash generator in the era.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.note: TI's role and the 7400/74S chronology are high confidence. Specific plant names are given as commonly-cited TI locations rather than verified suppliers of Commodore's lots.

facts.label: Extra business
facts.value: foundry / fab-forum for other semiconductor firms

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.name: Fairchild
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.description: The company where Faggin invented the silicon-gate technology that made CMOS practical, in 1968, and which shipped the first commercial silicon-gate MOS ICs. Fairchild went bankrupt in 1985 and its remaining operations were absorbed by National and by a French group, so by 1983 a Fairchild-branded 74LS was already a slightly awkward purchase.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.note: Fairchild's silicon-gate invention in 1968 and the 1985 bankruptcy are well documented. That Fairchild-branded logic was actually present on C64 boards is field-attested, but no specific board photograph showing it has been verified.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.name: National Semiconductor
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.description: A major second-source supplier of 74LS logic throughout the period, and the company that published the 74HC/74HCT databooks that turned high-speed CMOS into a genuine 74-series replacement. It later absorbed much of Fairchild.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.note: National as a 74LS supplier is high confidence. Its 74HC databooks (1983) are a well-documented and interesting artefact - the high-speed CMOS family arriving at the same moment as the C64.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.name: Motorola
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.description: The dominant supplier of the 4000-series CMOS parts on this board: the MC4044 phase comparator at U32 and the two MC4066 bilateral switches. The MC prefix on those parts is Motorola's, which is why the C64's glue logic is not entirely a 74-series story. Motorola also ran one of the merchant 74LS lines, and in 1969 it licensed and cross-supplied with Signetics, so the two names turned up in the same catalogue and the same distribution literature of the era.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.note: Motorola as the MC-prefix supplier of the 4066 and 4044 is high confidence - that is what the MC prefix means. The 1969 licensing and cross-supply arrangement with Signetics is well documented for that era, but no primary source is cited for it here.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics.name: Signetics
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics.description: An early Silicon Valley logic house that second-sourced the 74 series through the 1960s and 1970s, and that had been owned by Philips since 1975. It is not attested by name on surviving ASSY 250407 boards. It appears in this branch only because it shared a licensing and cross-supply arrangement with Motorola from 1969, which is why the two marks appear together in period catalogues and why repair literature treats them as a pair.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics.note: Low confidence, and deliberately so: no source is held for the Philips ownership date or for the 1969 arrangement, and a Signetics-branded part on a C64 mainboard is not verified.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.hitachi.name: Hitachi
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.hitachi.description: Japanese logic vendor. C64 boards are found with Hitachi-branded parts. Commodore bought early and often, and the rising Japanese share was one reason the C64's bill of materials got cheaper every year.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.hitachi.note: Low confidence on specific Hitachi parts appearing on 1983 C64 boards. A Hitachi-branded 74LS in a 250407 is an unverified field report; Japanese penetration of merchant logic through the decade is well documented.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.toshiba.name: Toshiba
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.toshiba.description: Japanese logic and semiconductor vendor, among the Japanese suppliers that took a large share of world logic volume through the 1980s, undercutting American silicon. No Toshiba-branded logic part on a 250407 is specifically verified here; included as the second named Japanese supplier alongside Hitachi.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.toshiba.note: Low confidence; no specific Toshiba-branded 74LS in a 250407 verified. General Japanese penetration well documented; split from makers.japan list so each supplier is its own org rather than a bundled list.
